items.title: The China Strategy Hollywood Doesn’t Want You to Know About
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Important.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A Hollywood producer who spent years courting China to support American film studios is now speaking out against Tinseltown’s attempts to work with the communist nation.

Christopher Fenton, producer of the new film, “Bad Counselors,” told CBN News Hollywood is always trying to find new businesses and new sources of capital to help make expensive films and projects possible.

“Then, on top of it, on the output side of things … once you actually get it into theaters, are there markets there that we haven’t explored?” he said, detailing the questions executives are often faced with. “Are there potential ways to generate new revenue?”

Decades ago, he said the U.S. approach to China started to shift, with America opening up more relations with the nation. While America initially had a “frozen relationship” with China, an idea took root: that the more products and services the U.S. could get into the nation, the “more we would spread the aspirational quality of democracy inside of a communist country.”

In addition to growing the economy in the U.S., Fenton said there was a higher mission and purpose in engaging China and opening up the market.

“What we found over time … is that aspirational quality of democracy inside a communist country plan hasn’t really worked out all that well,” he said.

Fenton said jobs were generated and GDP growth came, but that it was only a “sugar high” that didn’t last. Overall, he said Hollywood’s market share in China has been lost. The initial plans simply didn’t pan out the way he and others wanted.

“The initial thought was the more products and services we could get in that country, the better, no matter what it took to get them in,” he said. “So it was like an ends-justify-the-means plan.”

While 99% of people seeking to engage China in this way were looking to help the U.S., he said the other “1% was very willing to sell out the soul of America to make a buck.”

Regardless of the mission, there was an unintended consequence of the relationship between China and the U.S. — and it involved bias and a quest for the communist party to push its ideologies on the masses.

“For the most part, we were under this other higher mission,” he said. “And part of that for Beijing and the entertainment content space was to placate them and their directives in terms of messaging and narrative, the way they wanted their system of government presented to their own people to essentially make that 1.3 billion people just happy enough that they don’t revolt and have another Tiananmen Square incident like June 4, 1989.”

But it didn’t end there.

“Essentially they saw it as a propaganda engine in the West, this Hollywood content ecosystem,” Fenton said. “To essentially take and trumpet their messaging and narratives around the world.”

He cited the film “Looper,” which he produced, as an example. Fenton said the time-travel film initially depicted a future utopian society in France.

“But Beijing said, ‘If you want access to our market, you need to change your time travel story to one where China is the utopian place to live, where the weight of the world is shifting, and if you change the plot to be where everybody wants to be someday is China, we’ll let you have that movie in,'” Fenton said. “So we actually completely changed the script, completely changed the narrative to be pro-Beijing, pro-China in order to get access to that market.”

He continued, “It gave us a top 10 movie that year in the market, and no one else in the world noticed the fact that they were digesting propaganda from what was a pretty good movie.”

Fenton said this sort of dynamic might not be as prevalent right now as “the golden goose of China is sort of cooked right now,” with many people and businesses moving away from the communist country.

“This kind of propaganda, this kind of messaging, this kind of control over narrative globally is across all industries,” he said. “So yes, entertainment business is sort of the easiest one to see because we tell stories that prepare that narrative and messaging from Beijing, but it’s happening in all industries in the way they’re throttled on certain things they can say or the things that they really might not want to say or things that they need to trumpet are amplified and they’re pushed to amplify.”

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

He said these portrayals affect how young Americans view China, with some believing there are incredible buildings, skyscrapers, and happy people everywhere.

“They see nothing bad about China,” he said. “And it’s why we’re starting to see Pew studies show that people actually think more favorably in terms of China than they do the United States.”

This framing is one reason why Fenton is now pushing for films and projects to be made in America. His new film, “Bad Counselors,” is an example of a movie that was fully created here in the US.

“We wanted all American backdrops,” he said. “We shot in North Carolina. We did a little in Texas, a little in Tennessee. We used all vendors that were American and we fully employed Americans, your brethren, my brethren. We made sure that we took care of our citizens.”

The premise of “Bad Counselors” is comical — and very American.

“Two frat bros must become church bros, fast,” the synopsis reads. “After one wild night ends in handcuffs and a campus police escort, two best friends are slapped with 120 hours of community service due in two weeks, or they’re expelled. Their genius plan? Pose as counselors at a local Christian youth camp, where every sing-along, campfire devotional, and trust fall counts toward the clock. Just one problem (okay, three): they don’t like kids, they hate camping, and they have barely set foot in a church.”

items.title: ‘Craving the Truth’: The Shocking Spiritual Hunger Sweeping Gen Z
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Naomi Anderson is on a mission to point Generation Z toward the truth.

Anderson is co-founder of Verity Collective, “a movement rooted in the unchanging truth of the Gospel.” She told CBN News she wants to bring Jesus to America’s young generation.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

“We believe that there is a lot of confusion and noise in this world for them, and we want to bring them back to the one and only truth, which is Jesus,” she said.

Anderson believes young people are “craving the truth” but have faced an uphill battle in understanding it, as they’ve been sold an improper understanding of reality.

“They are craving the truth. They just don’t know what it is because they’ve been told to define it for themselves,” she said. “So when we ask them, ‘What is truth?’ they literally will sit there on camera and it will take them minutes to try to decide right because they have been told truth is objective — you can define your own truth. … They just need to be pointed back to the truth.”

The need for truth couldn’t be more pressing, as many young people are suffering from mental health issues, including anxiety and depression.

“It all forms around this idea of what is my identity, and where am I grounded in, and they just don’t have a landing solid spot,” Anderson said.

She also noted that young men appear to be increasingly interested in the Christian faith.

“These men are craving solid biblical truth, and that only comes from reading your Bible, and picking up the word, and being taught it by a Bible teacher,” Anderson said.

Through Verity Collective, she’s hoping to visit college campuses across the US in September and have a presence to spark conversations.

“What we’re recognizing is that when you actually pull someone aside and start asking them questions like, ‘What is truth?’ they have a yearning to know what it is that you want them to know,” Anderson said. “They’ll ask … ‘What do you believe truth is?’ And it really does open up an opportunity for us to speak the Gospel of Jesus Christ to them. And they are excited to hear it.”

items.title: God’s Better Country
items.author: Amy Boucher Pye
items.summary: Michele experienced a mixture of emotions as her father neared the end of his life. She grieved when he said, “Honey, I won’t be here to walk you down the aisle.” But she assured him of her love, clinging to the hope she found in Hebrews 11 as she said: “You’re heading
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Michele experienced a mixture of emotions as her father neared the end of his life. She grieved when he said, “Honey, I won’t be here to walk you down the aisle.” But she assured him of her love, clinging to the hope she found in Hebrews 11 as she said: “You’re heading for a better country, a country in heaven.” Michele believed that her dad, when he died, would be with God forever. She reflected, “Heaven will be that good!”

The letter to the Hebrews was aimed at the Jewish believers experiencing persecution by state and religious opponents. Although it was written before the destruction of the temple in ad 70, the fall of Jerusalem to the Romans may have occurred soon after. In this climate of fear, the author urged the believers to hold firm to their faith as he highlighted a great “cloud of witnesses” (Hebrews 12:1). Each “did not receive the things promised; they only saw them and welcomed them from a distance” (Hebrews 11:13). They lived by faith, “longing for a better country—a heavenly one.” God was pleased to be called their God, and He “prepared a city for them” (v. 16).

Although Michele ached with sadness when her father died, she embraced the promises of her heavenly Father. We too can welcome these same promises “from a distance” (v. 13), trusting in God.

items.title: The Battle Is God’s
items.author: Leslie Koh
items.summary: Though she enjoyed befriending and helping folks in her church’s seniors ministry, Carol found herself being picked on by its domineering leader. She felt so bothered by it that she had to seek counseling. She was advised to quit the ministry, but she didn’t want to “abandon”
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Though she enjoyed befriending and helping folks in her church’s seniors ministry, Carol found herself being picked on by its domineering leader. She felt so bothered by it that she had to seek counseling. She was advised to quit the ministry, but she didn’t want to “abandon” the seniors. Feeling caught in between, she prayed to God for guidance, and He gave her comfort and assurance as she submitted her fears to Him. He showed her that she should talk to the leader but trust Him to resolve the issue.

When King Jehoshaphat heard of a powerful enemy approaching Jerusalem, his first response was to pray. Appealing to God’s sovereignty, he said: “We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you” (2 Chronicles 20:12). Instead of relying on their own strength, the king and people of Judah submitted themselves and their troubles to God.

God’s answer was heartening: “Do not be afraid or discouraged . . . . For the battle is not yours, but God’s” (v. 15). God commanded Judah to march out, but to trust Him with the result. They did so in faith, praising God as if the prayer was already answered—and found a battle already won (vv. 20-21, 24).

Whenever we face difficult situations, let’s pray and look to God for help. We may not always see victory, but whatever happens, we need not be afraid, for the battle is His.

items.title: Polaroid’s New Ad Campaign Takes a Shot at AI — and the Internet Is Cheering
items.author: Emily Brown
items.summary: Polaroid has figured out the easiest way to win over the internet: Tell everyone to get off the internet. The camera company’s latest campaign, “The Best of Summer Is Analog,” is built around a series of billboards encouraging people to put down their phones and experience something that cannot be g
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Polaroid has figured out the easiest way to win over the internet: Tell everyone to get off the internet.

The camera company’s latest campaign, “The Best of Summer Is Analog,” is built around a series of billboards encouraging people to put down their phones and experience something that cannot be generated, optimized or turned into content.

“You can’t bask in blue light,” one ad reads. Another offers a revised version of familiar advice: “Dance like nobody is recording.”

The sharpest billboard appeared on Coney Island Beach with a slightly more ominous suggestion: “Go jump in some water before the data centers drink it all up.” Other ads sarcastically celebrate “a glorious day to stare into various screens for hours on end.” The campaign is running across New York, London and South Korea as part of the launch of Polaroid’s Go Generation 3 instant camera.

Naturally, screenshots of the campaign immediately spread across the screens it was criticizing. A post featuring the ads became the biggest thread across r/popculturechat this week, earning nearly 29,000 upvotes as commenters celebrated Polaroid for saying what an increasingly exhausted online generation has apparently been thinking.

Yes, this is still an advertisement. Polaroid would very much like people to respond to their digital fatigue by purchasing a camera. But the pitch is landing because it understands something bigger than film photography: People are tired of living as though every meaningful experience must also become digital evidence.

AI has only sharpened the unease. Now the internet is not merely documenting reality. It is manufacturing an endless supply of images, songs, videos and people who never existed. The result is a strange cultural moment in which the imperfect has started to feel more valuable precisely because it proves someone was actually there.

Polaroid’s creative director, Patricia Varella, said the company found its campaign when it stopped asking how to make instant cameras appealing to Gen Z and started asking why Polaroid should exist at all in an AI-dominated culture.

“For Polaroid, the simple act of existing is already an act of rebellion,” Varella said. “While our campaigns are provocative and challenge our relationship with technology, we’re not anti-digital. We know we have to live alongside it, but we’re deeply pro-human.”

Feature-Length Documentary Explores the Beauty, History, and Theology of

ROCHESTER, Minn., & DENVER, Colo. — July 31, 2026 — Tickets are now on sale for Heaven in Stone and Glass, Bishop Robert Barron’s new feature-length documentary that brings audiences inside five of France’s most magnificent Gothic cathedrals during a special two-night theatrical release on Sept. 20 and 23, 2026.

Produced by Word on Fire in collaboration with Spirit Juice Studios, the immersive cinematic experience combines breathtaking photography with Bishop Barron’s signature theological storytelling. Heaven in Stone and Glass is being distributed by Fathom Entertainment, the leading specialty distributor of content to theatrical partners worldwide.

Filmed on location throughout France, Heaven in Stone and Glass explores Notre-Dame, Chartres, Reims, Amiens, and Saint-Denis, revealing the extraordinary artistry and theological meaning woven into each cathedral. Beginning with the aftermath of the 2019 Notre-Dame fire, Bishop Barron guides audiences through centuries of history, Scripture, philosophy, and architecture, demonstrating how these enduring masterpieces continue to proclaim the Christian vision through beauty.

“These cathedrals still have something to say to our culture,” said Bishop Robert Barron. “They were built to lift the mind and heart toward God, and they continue to speak a language of beauty that transcends every generation. My hope is that audiences leave the theatre with renewed wonder—not only at these extraordinary buildings but at the God of wonder himself.”

Heaven in Stone and Glass marks Word on Fire’s first nationwide theatrical release and continues Bishop Barron’s acclaimed tradition of bringing the richness of the Catholic intellectual tradition to audiences through visually stunning documentary filmmaking. His previous productions include the internationally celebrated CATHOLICISM and Pivotal Players series.

Designed for audiences of faith, history enthusiasts, architecture lovers, and anyone drawn to stories of art and culture, Heaven in Stone and Glass offers a rare opportunity to experience some of the world’s greatest sacred spaces through an immersive theatrical presentation.

Tickets for Heaven in Stone and Glass are available now online and at participating theatre box offices. (Theatre locations are subject to change.) For more information, please visit FathomEntertainment.com.

items.title: ‘Toy Story 5’ Helps Us Cultivate Wonder Anew
items.author: Dr. LuElla D’Amico
items.summary:
Dr. LuElla D’Amico

Wonder is not merely found in childhood. It is cultivated there. And perhaps that is one way we become like little children again.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. LuElla D’Amico

I was eleven when the first Toy Story came out—about the same age as the movie’s protagonist, Andy, and one year younger than my son is now. He has always been more than a little obsessed with the Toy Story films. What is probably no surprise to those who know me well is that I was the sort of girl who continued playing with dolls a little longer than most. My Barbies, together with an assortment of stuffed animals, lived elaborate lives filled with high drama. There were weddings and mysteries, betrayals and reconciliations, daring rescues and last-minute plot twists. My bedroom floor became an entire world. As Anne Shirley would say, there was always “scope for the imagination” whenever there were dolls nearby. My son—who may someday begrudge reading this but would no doubt concede its truth—is not much different.

It is little surprise, then, that my favorite moments in Toy Story 5 appear in both its opening and closing scenes. Bonnie’s toys are swept into one of her wonderfully overcomplicated adventures involving romance, villains, explosions, weddings, and all the joyful chaos only a child can invent. Watching those scenes, I felt immediate recognition. The film captures imaginative play not merely with affection but with remarkable attentiveness to the way children actually inhabit the world. They are loving, but they are also chaotic. If Bonnie’s playtime had a theater marquee, it might read: “Love! Drama! Mystery! Heroism! Intrigue! Impossible Rescues!” Every object she touches suddenly possesses a double life. Every room becomes a kingdom waiting to be explored. Somehow, through all of it, the ordinary world begins to shimmer with something larger than itself. I have come to believe that imagination is one of our first steps toward transcendence.

For readers who have not yet seen the film, Toy Story 5 follows eight-year-old Bonnie as she grows increasingly attached to Lilypad, an interactive device designed to educate, entertain, and accompany children through nearly every part of the day. Jessie, Bonnie’s beloved cowgirl toy, fears history is repeating itself. Once loved by her first owner, Emily, and later abandoned when childhood passed, Jessie worries Bonnie is beginning to outgrow her as well. What follows is less a battle between good and evil than between two visions of childhood: one increasingly mediated by technology and another sustained by imagination, friendship, and play.

The contrast is striking. Each time Bonnie plays with Jessie and the other toys, she leaves animated, laughing, and utterly absorbed in the world she has created. Each time she spends hours with Lilypad, by contrast, she seems noticeably more drained—a difference obvious to the audience even if Bonnie herself cannot yet perceive it. The toys notice it, too. After one especially elaborate adventure, Jessie can only stare in amazement before breaking into one of her exuberant “Yee-haws!” The toys have not simply entertained Bonnie; they have participated in a world she imagined into being. The film suggests that the difference is not merely between two forms of entertainment. One consumes Bonnie’s attention; the other calls forth her imagination. With Lilypad, Bonnie receives a finished world. With Jessie, she becomes its author.

As viewers, we experience something similar. Children watching the film likely recognize their own games reflected on the screen. Adults perhaps remember their own childhood play—and something else besides: Wonder is not merely found in childhood. It is cultivated there.

Watching Bonnie’s imaginative adventures, I found myself returning to C. S. Lewis’s essay “On Three Ways of Writing for Children,” Lewis argues that the best stories for children arise from the part of the adult imagination that still delights in the same things children love. Adults differ from children not because they have abandoned wonder but because wonder now lives alongside many other interests. The best children’s stories—and movies, I would add—remind us that imagination is not something we are meant to discard with age.

Around the time the first Toy Story was released, I began wondering whether my own enthusiasm for imaginative play was something I ought to outgrow. The other girls around me seemed to move on more easily. They wanted to talk about dating and middle school social life while I still wanted to invent stories. I knew St. Paul had written, “When I became an adult, I put an end to childish ways” (1 Cor 13:11), and I wondered whether I was late in doing so.

Looking back, I realize I misunderstood St. Paul. First Corinthians is a meditation on maturity in love, not an argument against wonder. The chapter concludes by reminding us that “faith, hope, and love abide, these three; and the greatest of these is love.” Long before I could explain those virtues, I was practicing them through stories. My dolls taught me to imagine reconciliation before I understood forgiveness, courage before I encountered suffering, and hope before life gave me reasons to need it. Play was never an escape from reality. It was one of the first ways I learned to love reality.

Perhaps that is why, when my son started kindergarten, he insisted on carrying a Woody backpack to school despite never having seen a Toy Story movie. My husband wisely observed that if Woody was going to accompany our son every day, perhaps our son ought to know who Woody actually was. One of his earliest trips to the movie theater became Toy Story 3. Before long, our living room was filled with Woody, Buzz, Jessie, Rex, Hamm, and Bullseye undertaking adventures that bore only passing resemblance to the films themselves. Now, the movies may have supplied the characters, but my son supplied the stories.

Screens can tell wonderful stories; toys invite children to become storytellers.

Ironically, seeing Toy Story 3 in the theater was something of an anomaly in our house. Like many young parents, I was determined to do everything “right.” Screen time was tightly limited. We read books before bed. Toys lived in baskets rather than on tablets. I imagined that enough intentional parenting could largely determine the influences shaping my children.

Then life happened.

When the pandemic arrived, I was teaching college courses through Zoom while my son completed first grade from our dining room table. Church, birthday parties, Scout meetings, visits with grandparents, and ordinary conversations with friends were suddenly mediated through glowing rectangles. Technology was no longer simply a convenience; it became the infrastructure of daily life.

I remain grateful for it, though. Without those devices, many of us would have endured those pandemic years in profound isolation. Screens allowed my students to continue learning, my son to remain connected to classmates, and families to see loved ones they could not visit. Technology served a deeply human purpose.

Yet once the crisis passed, many of those habits remained. Families like mine had not consciously decided that screens should occupy so much of our lives. They simply had. The tools that had served us so well became the place where work, school, entertainment, shopping, conversation, and leisure increasingly occurred. As Woody observes early in the film, “Toys are for play, but tech is . . . tech is for everything.” 

Our phones have become maps, calendars, cameras, libraries, classrooms, televisions, and conversation partners. Their strength lies precisely in their versatility. Yet because they can do so much, they also threaten to crowd out slower practices that have long formed us.

That, I think, is the real concern of Toy Story 5. The film is not a Luddite’s dream. Lilypad is never portrayed as malicious. On the contrary, she genuinely wants what is best for Bonnie. She listens, learns, and eventually helps Bonnie meet Blaze, another imaginative child who becomes a real friend.

In other words, technology helps create communion, but it cannot sustain it.

And once Bonnie and Blaze meet, the screen recedes into the background. Indeed, the girls immediately begin doing what children have always done. They imagine. They laugh. They invent stories together. Technology has served its purpose by bringing them together, but friendship itself requires presence. This concluding segment of the movie strikes me as one resplendent with Catholic ideals about encounter and the value of human dignity.

In his recent encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, Pope Leo XIV reflects on the extraordinary promise of artificial intelligence while warning that technological progress must never eclipse “the grandeur of humanity.” The question is not whether we should develop extraordinary tools but whether those tools continue to serve the human person. (Watching Bonnie and Blaze meet one another face-to-face, leaving the screens behind, I could not help but think that this was precisely the sort of ordinary, embodied encounter the pope had in mind.) After all, our task is “to remain profoundly human,” he asserts, in this era of artificial intelligence.

How do we remain “profoundly human” when technology increasingly becomes “for everything,” as Woody put it? 

It might help to recall here that Catholics have long understood that we are formed by practices. We gather around tables. We keep holy days. We kneel. We pray. We sing. We receive Christ in the appearance of bread and wine rather than merely think about communion. Love is not sustained accidentally. It is cultivated.

Driving home from the theater with my now-twelve-year-old son, I realized the film had given us far more than a conversation about screens. It had reminded us of something we had, at least in my family, allowed to slip away over time without cognitively realizing it simply because we had not attended to making a habit of it. During the pandemic, technology entered our lives out of necessity. Afterward, it remained out of habit. Somewhere along the way, evenings increasingly ended with each of us retreating to our own devices—not because we loved one another any less but because that had become our default. Somewhere along the way, we had stopped playing together. Our stories were increasingly being told by our devices instead of by—and with—one another.

So, when we got home that evening, we made a different choice. We put our phones away.

We talked about Jessie and Woody. We laughed about Bonnie’s wonderfully ridiculous adventures. We imagined what the toys might do next. I won’t lie, it was hardly a dramatic family transformation. By the next morning, our phones were still there, our work still awaited us, and technology still occupied a place in our homes. We’re trying to become more intentional about wonder. Family game nights are back. So are screen limits. More importantly, we’re making room simply to play together again.

Perhaps that is why Jesus tells his disciples, “Unless you change and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt 18:3). He is not asking us to become childish. He is inviting us to recover the openness to wonder that children receive so naturally and adults must intentionally cultivate.

In an age when technology is “for everything,” perhaps Christians have an opportunity—and even a responsibility—to protect the practices that keep us fully human. Wonder is not merely found in childhood. It is cultivated there. And perhaps that is one way we become like little children again.

As Jessie reminds her friends, “Our time ain’t over yet.”
